articles.title: Man's secret use of synthetic testosterone for cows nearly destroyed his heart
articles.text:
For 11 years, a Massachusetts man had an alarming array of health problems, most notably that his heart kept failing. He landed in the hospital over and over again, needed life support at one point, spent years going to specialists, and underwent a barrage of tests along the way.

But through it all, he never revealed a key detail behind his ailments: He was taking powerful, illicit synthetic testosterone derivatives (aka anabolic-androgenic steroids, or AAS). One of the drugs he took was approved only for use in animals; it's primarily used to beef up cows.

Left in the dark, his doctors had to puzzle this out on their own. In a case report in this week's issue of the New England Journal of Medicine, they explain how they did it. They also offer a warning: These cases will only become more common, and clinicians need to know what they look like.

articles.title: New Facilities To Pump Out Upgraded F/A-18E/F Super Hornets Eyed By Navy
articles.text:
The U.S. Navy is looking for new avenues to bolster its pipelines for major F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and EA-18G Growler modifications. The prime contractor for that work now, Boeing, is in the process of expanding and reorganizing its production infrastructure. At the same time, the company’s defense business arm is also heavily focused on ramping up output of new aircraft, including the sixth-generation F-47 for the U.S. Air Force and the Navy’s next-generation carrier-based F/A-XX fighter.

Naval Air Systems Command (NAVAIR) is now “conducting market research to determine the industrial base’s existing capability and facility capacity to provide supplemental or secondary Service Life Modification (SLM) turnkey capacity for F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and EA-18G Growler aircraft starting in FY29 [Fiscal Year 2029],” according to a contracting notice put out earlier this week. “To support long-term strike fighter inventory requirements, the Government is evaluating the availability of additional commercial or second-source depot modification repair overhaul (MRO) capacity.”

Currently, Boeing performs Service Life Modification (SLM) work on Navy F/A-18E/Fs at facilities in St. Louis, Missouri, and San Antonio, Texas. The Navy has its own Super Hornet SLM line, operated in cooperation with Boeing, at the Fleet Readiness Center Southwest (FRCSW) depot in San Diego, California. Boeing conducts additional F/A-18E/F and EA-18G modification work at various facilities, including an additional site in Jacksonville, Florida.

In September 2025, Boeing announced its intention to shut down the SLM line in St. Louis in 2027 and transition at least some of that workload elsewhere, possibly to San Antonio and/or Jacksonville. The company also plans to end production of new Super Hornets in 2027. The EA-18G is already out of production.

The Navy still plans to put most, if not all, of its F/A-18E/Fs – a total fleet of approximately 550 aircraft at present – through the SLM process, and that work is expected to continue in the mid-2030s. SLM extends the service life of Super Hornets from 6,000 to 10,000 flight hours. The jets also receive Block III upgrades, including new wide-area touchscreen multifunction displays, major boosts in onboard networking capability and computer processing power, and an improved avionics suite.

Work is also now underway on a Block II upgrade package for the Navy’s roughly 160 EA-18Gs, which is set to include major improvements to the Growler’s electronic warfare suite.

Overall, “PMA-265 [the F/A-18E/F and EA-18G Program Office] anticipates a maximum SLM induction profile of up to 47 aircraft per year across the industrial base,” according to the recent NAVAIR contracting notice. “Actual aircraft allocation among available sources may vary based on Fleet requirements, aircraft availability, demonstrated performance, schedule, and available capacity.”

It is not immediately clear whether the 47-aircraft-per-year target represents a major increase in expected SLM throughput. Back in 2020, the Navy said its goal was to be inducting 40 Super Hornets into the SLM pipeline annually within three years. There was no indication at that time that this figure included any SLM and/or other upgrade work on its Growlers.

As noted earlier, this all comes amid a shakeup in Boeing’s physical infrastructure driven heavily by the new production demands, including those tied to the F-47 and F/A-XX. Industrial base capacity has been a major talking point when it comes to both of these sixth-generation fighter programs. The Pentagon previously attempted to shelve F/A-XX indefinitely, explicitly over concern about it competing for resources with F-47. Congress subsequently intervened to keep the Navy program going, leading to the contract award to Boeing in September.

Boeing is also now working to ramp up deliveries of F-15EX Eagle II fighters and T-7A jet trainers to the U.S. Air Force, as well as MQ-25 tanker drones to the U.S. Navy. The Air Force notably announced earlier this year that it had roughly doubled the number of F-15EXs it plans to acquire in total.

“Our expansion plans across the St. Louis site triggered the execution of a multi-year strategic plan, requiring the relocation of some work,” Dan Gillian, Vice President and General Manager of Air Dominance at Boeing, had said in a statement accompanying last year’s announcement about plans to move Super Hornet SLM work to other locations. “Given we are already successfully conducting SLM at other locations, this move is logical so we can continue to meet our customers commitments while ensuring we are well poised for future work.”

“Delivering two advanced fighters in parallel was always our plan, and we invested accordingly,” Steve Parker, President and CEO of Boeing Defense, Space & Security, said in a statement after the company won the F/A-XX competition. “We are ready and able to build multiple concurrent future combat aircraft franchise programs.”

F/A-XX is expected to eventually replace the Navy’s F/A-18E/F and EA-18G fleets, but the first of those next-generation fighters are not expected to begin entering service until some time in the 2030s. As such, Super Hornets and Growlers look set to continue being the primary workhorses of the service’s carrier air wings for years to come.

F/A-18E/F and EA-18G have been key players in the ongoing war with Iran, as well as other recent conflicts in the Middle East. Both types were also part of the larger force package that supported the operation to capture Venezuelan dictator Nicolas Maduro, and had been operating in the Caribbean for months beforehand as part of the U.S. military build-up in the region.

In turn, ensuring that there are no major disruptions to the SLM process and other upgrades for the F/A-18E/F and EA-18G will continue to be a priority for the Navy, as underscored now by the recent NAVAIR contracting notice. The possibility of the F/A-18E/F fleet receiving additional significant upgrades in the future, particularly to extend their range, has also been raised in the past. The arsenal of munitions available to the Navy’s Super Hornet is also growing substantially. This includes a still-expanding array of longer-range air-to-air missiles, as well as hypersonic Blackbeard air-to-surface missiles.

Just expanding the Super Hornet/Growler SLM/upgrade pipeline could open up interesting new opportunities for companies beyond Boeing. Northrop Grumman, which lost in the F/A-XX competition, has been involved in Super Hornet production in the past as a subcontractor. The Navy might also be interested in tapping new firms, including ones that are already working to expand their defense industrial presence, rather than long-established prime defense contractors.

“We have worked with the Navy for years to improve SLM while growing in San Antonio and FRC Southwest,” Mark Sears, Boeing Fighters Vice President, also said last year. “Delivering multiple fighters and capabilities from multiple locations is what we do, and we will continue that work on the Super Hornets for the life of the fleet.”

NAVAIR’s recent announcement makes clear that the Navy is still very much in the early phases of determining what, if any, new courses of action it ultimately wants to take regarding SLM and other upgrade work for its F/A-18E/F and EA-18G fleets. That being said, new facilities to support those efforts, potentially with new contractors running them, may now be on the horizon

articles.title: The amazing disappearing exoplanet
articles.text:
One nice thing about discovering exoplanets is that, once you work out how long their orbits take, they continue to show up like clockwork. The timing is so regular, in fact, that we can use variations to detect the gravitational influence of additional planets in the same exosolar system. And the precise timing is useful in that we can rely on it to point telescopes at the system when we know some of the light we detect has passed through the planet's atmosphere.

Except when we can't.

On Monday, researchers reported on an exoplanet that simply stopped showing up. TOI-2535b is a hot Jupiter-sized planet we've been observing as it transits between its host star, TOI-2535, and Earth for about seven years now. But it recently stopped showing up, and researchers suspect that's due to an unseen companion orbiting in a different plane.

articles.title: Pakistan-Based Gangster Under NIA Scanner Over Youth Radicalisation
articles.text:
The National Investigation Agency has registered a case to probe the online radicalisation of Indian youths by Pakistan-based gangster Shahzad Bhatti and other ISI agents with the intention to carry out terror attacks in the country, officials said on Thursday.
The probe stems from a case registered by the Uttar Pradesh Anti-Terrorist Squad (ATS) in April this year.
The FIR named eight accused in the case, including Bhatti, an Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI) agent based in Pakistan. ISI is Pakistan’s spy agency.
The central government had in September this year declared the Pakistan-based Shahzad Bhatti Network (SBN) a terrorist organisation under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.
The action was taken as the Centre believed that the SBN was involved in “terrorism and has participated in various acts of terrorism in India.” Others named as accused in the NIA’s First Information Report (FIR) included Md Hamad Barkati, Abid Jatt, Major Hamid, Major Iqbal — all of whom are ISI agents — and one Major Anwar based in Pakistan.
The NIA also named Tushar Chauhan alias Hijbullah Ali Khan, a resident of Uttar Pradesh, and Sameer, a resident of Delhi, as accused in the case. The two were arrested by the UP ATS in April this year.
The Uttar Pradesh ATS, investigating the presence of Pakistani sleeper cells created through social media, had found that these two men were allegedly in direct contact with Pakistani operatives and “planning a major disruptive act”.
During the investigation, it emerged that Pakistani gangster Bhatti, Jatt and radical Pakistani YouTubers, allegedly acting on instructions from the ISI, were attempting to radicalise Indian youths and entice them with financial incentives to disturb internal peace and communal harmony, Uttar Pradesh’s Additional Director General of Police (Law and Order) Amitabh Yash had said.

articles.title: Microsoft has an image problem with November's Windows security update
articles.text:
Printing with Windows has always been something of a choose-your-own-adventure, and November's security update has added another unwelcome plot twist: documents containing certain images might not print.

The issue affects images rendered with a height or width of zero at the selected printing resolution. These might not be visible to users, but can form part of a document's watermarking or layout.

After the update, those invisible objects can apparently make the printed document disappear too. Microsoft said: "The issue was observed when printing Microsoft Word documents using the Windows Graphics Device Interface (GDI), but printing from other applications might also be affected."

According to the notification (WI1549472), most versions of Windows are affected, from the latest Windows 11 26H2 through Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2016. Windows Server from 2025 to 2016 is also affected.

Users need not have added these objects themselves. Microsoft says document-generation tools can insert them even when no graphic is visible.

Printer problems aren't the only issue requiring attention. After installation of the November 2026 security update, Microsoft warned that "certain Windows activation and licensing operations performed using the Software Licensing Management Tool (SLMGR) might fail."

This one is a little more niche, but it could be a headache for affected administrators. It primarily affects organizations that use command-line tools or automated processes to manage Windows activation and licensing.

"Affected devices might encounter error 0x80041008, Invalid parameter (SWbemObjectEx), when running commands to activate Windows, configure Key Management Service (KMS), or manage product keys," Microsoft said. "The failure has been observed while executing the command 'slmgr.vbs /skms-domain' and 'slmgr.vbs /ipk'."

The notice (WI1549486) currently lists Windows 11 23H2, Windows 10 22H2 and 21H2, and Windows Server 2025, 2022, and 2019 as affected.

The printing problem remains under investigation, but Microsoft says a fix for the activation issue is due in the coming days. Administrators needing an interim workaround must contact Microsoft Support for Business. ®

articles.title: Jensen Huang is out. What did China want from him?
articles.text:
Today, we’re talking about the Jensen Huang scandal at Nvidia, which is developing so quickly that we had to do an emergency update of this intro minutes before publishing this episode.

Huang just resigned from his position as CEO of Nvidia as news of his affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, threatened to engulf the company.

We’ll have more on that story as things develop and we learn how Nvidia will restructure itself after Jensen — he had something like 60 direct reports, after all, and the entire AI financial ecosystem flows through the company. This is pure Decoder bait.

But just two days ago I talked to Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, about the real heart of the scandal: What would China even seek to accomplish by having a spy so close to Jensen? And what does the real state of the US-China AI conflict really looks like, particularly from the Chinese point of view?

Kyle’s answers about chips and how China is perceiving the so-called AI “race” were very illuminating, but maybe even more interesting was his observation on Jensen Huang’s relationship with Trump was the most important thing of all — because maybe what China most stood to gain was someone who could whisper in the right ears.

Let’s just dive right into it. But keep in mind that when we were talking, we still didn’t know what would happen with Jensen.

Okay: Kyle Chan on Nvidia, China, and the future of AI export controls. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Kyle Chan, you are a fellow at the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution. Welcome to Decoder.

Great to be here.

What on earth could we be talking about as it relates to your expertise about China today? I have a lot to ask you about Nvidia, about our relationship to China as a country, as an economy, and about national security.

Let’s start at the very beginning. From all the reporting we have today, it seems like the United States government has been very worried about a company called Megaspeed and Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy at the center of the swirling scandal around Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia. What do we know about Alice Huang and Megaspeed?

We have to be careful about what we know and what we don’t know. So far, there are allegations that the US intelligence community believes that Alice Huang may be an asset of the Chinese intelligence services. Megaspeed itself is a customer of Nvidia’s and they built a data center in Malaysia.

They also seem to potentially have ties with Chinese companies and could — and this is where we’re getting into what we do know and what we don’t know — potentially be a conduit for Chinese AI companies accessing cutting-edge Nvidia chips like Blackwells.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

I want to rewind way back. The notion that the Chinese AI industry wants Nvidia chips has been floating around for years and the idea that the Chinese AI industry would somehow develop a parallel set of technology or a superior set of technology because of the constraint of not having Nvidia chips has percolated into the discourse several times.

I’m particularly thinking about DeepSeek. DeepSeek launched R1 and it outperformed our models in some ways. We think they didn’t have access to the chips. There are some accusations that they had access to the chips. It turns out they did a bunch of fine-tuning on the chips they did have.

What is that relationship like? Do they need the highest-end Nvidia chips? Is it true that they’re actually developing parallel technologies that might be superior to the chips they can have? Just set that stage.

A lot of the details are murky, and they’re probably murky for a reason. But up until now, we saw Chinese AI companies that were very heavily dependent on Nvidia chips in order to train and run their models. In fact, they became some of the biggest contributors to the CUDA ecosystem, which is Nvidia’s software ecosystem and platform.

They got very good at that, but at the same time with US export controls and greater technology restrictions on access to cutting-edge GPUs, China increasingly pushed these AI companies to switch away from Nvidia to Huawei and other domestic AI chip makers. The idea there is to develop a parallel domestic AI chip supply chain that is good enough, if not on par with, Nvidia’s latest chips, and — crucially — resilient to policy actions coming out of Washington.

So that is the story up until this point. The question is, now, what is that trajectory for the Chinese GPU or AI chip development?

The reason I wanted to start there is that the motivations to get close to Jensen Huang are very murky to me. As the CEO of Nvidia, I understand that everyone thinks he’s the character and he’s actually in the software designing the next generation of Nvidia GPUs, but he’s just traveling the world giving policy speeches.

If you want to build a parallel GPU ecosystem, you’re trying to get close to the designers and the engineers, right? What would be the goal of trying to get close to Jensen Huang?

If you wanted the design specs for the latest Nvidia GPUs, I don’t know if you would ask Jensen directly. I think you might want to go to his technical staff.

He does have like 60 direct reports. Decoder is often a show about org charts and that one has been on top of my list for a long time, but we’ll set that aside for now. Keep going.

What it’s really about is potentially two things. One is trying to understand, maybe to glean information about, the US policymaking process. Jensen Huang is very close to Trump. They talk a lot. Trump can apparently just call Jensen on his cell phone at any moment.

In the middle of a conference. We’ve seen the video.

On the other side, and maybe this is even the bigger issue, perhaps it’s the biggest concern of all, is the concern that the direction of movement could run the other way, which is that somehow through Jensen, China might be able to influence US policymaking, especially on export controls. That is the big worry from a lot of people in Washington.

One of the other underlying concerns here, that I’m just trying to parse out, is that Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy, is an executive at a company called Megaspeed. And through Megaspeed, Nvidia may have already been circumventing export controls.

It seems like if you’re already solving the problem, maybe you should just leave it alone. How does that dynamic play out?

A lot of the story is strange. Even seen in the most cynical terms, it doesn’t quite add up. There could be several different possibilities. One is that this is actually not some concerted strategy from Beijing to try to obtain chips or information or influence, but this is potentially Beijing not quite understanding the full situation and wanting to co-op this Alice Huang person and at least try to understand from her standpoint what is happening.

Because I think you’re right. Already you have a very strong relationship between Nvidia and Megaspeed. You also already have — and this is on the influence side — Jensen Huang advocating for his own commercial interests, for a loosening of export controls on his own chips to China. You don’t really need Beijing to push on that gas pedal. That’s already happening.

So there are some things that don’t quite make sense if you’re thinking about it from those standpoints, but if you’re thinking about it from the viewpoint of “Beijing wants visibility,” then perhaps that is another plausible explanation.

Beijing just wants someone who Trump calls on the phone to advocate for their viewpoints. I see all of that, but what are we getting out of it? If the goal is Nvidia chips, it feels like that is already assured. If the goal is Nvidia engineering plans, that feels like a question mark. If the goal is influence over the Trump administration, I feel like they could have just bought cryptocurrency.

[Laughs] That’s right.

There’s a big swirl of what is actually happening here. Maybe your point that Beijing just needed more visibility because it is a swirl is the motivating factor. The question that leads me to is that the New York Times reports that US intelligence agencies first flagged these issues a year ago to the Trump administration. There was a memo from Marco Rubio. The reporting is that he oversaw the memo, which is as much plausible deniability as anything. He oversaw it. He was aware that there was a memo. A year ago, the United States’ national security apparatus was worried about Alice Huang at Megaspeed, her relationship with Jensen, and nothing occurred. What do you make of that?

That is one of the most worrying aspects of all this. Regardless of what the details are and what is known publicly versus what our intelligence community knows, this is something that should be investigated. This is obviously a major national security issue and this is something where you don’t want someone meddling with this process. You want to do a full investigation, get to the bottom of what’s happening.

I think what we’re seeing from some of the reporting is that this has been known, and in fact, if anything, there may have been efforts to try to stop this investigation or distort it in some way. That is very troubling from that internal, within-the-US-government perspective.

There’s a lot going on with Nvidia in that part of the story, where Nvidia’s own spokespeople are saying, “There’s nothing going on here. This is a normal relationship,” on the record to many publications. A week later, Jensen issues his apology letter saying there was a relationship.

That’s not great for John Rizzo, Nvidia’s comms person. Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, is out there saying everything is above board. Now we know not everything is above board. What do you make of Nvidia’s corporate governance here? Because there’s a whole bunch of shareholder lawsuits to come. There’s one filed as of today. I can only imagine there are more to come.

Nvidia has to tread very carefully here because what you don’t want is exactly what’s already happening, which is to start to deny or dismiss some of these issues and then turn around and have to say, “Actually, there might be something there.”

This is especially important now as there are growing calls for a congressional investigation. So this is going to be separate, perhaps, from within the executive branch where, again, I think we have reasons to worry about conflicts of interest and people not wanting to do this all the way. But if there’s a full-blown congressional investigation, that might reveal some things that, if you are Nvidia, you want to get out in front of rather than have to backpedal later on and explain yourself.

Part of the back and forth here with the government’s concern about Alice Huang and Megaspeed is that the Commerce Department spent months looking at the company and then Teter, the general counsel of Nvidia, emailed them and invoked a direct relationship with the Commerce undersecretary, Jeff Kessler. That got the case kicked to the DOJ where everything stopped.

Trump yesterday said the FBI is investigating — that’s obviously connected to the DOJ. There’s a universe where the Trump administration is trying to make this go away. Nvidia can pressure the Trump administration to make this go away. That reeks of corruption, obviously.

And then you have a very empowered class of Democrats coming into Congress with polling that suggested corruption was one of the top issues in this last election. I don’t see any outcome except those Democrats and an empowered bunch of investigators and an empowered bunch of committee chairs coming after Nvidia as hard as they can.

How should the company think about that? Should they just fire Jensen now to get away from it? Should they put them in front of Congress every day for the next year? How do you think that’s going to play out?

I think, at the most fundamental level, they need to cooperate and comply with calls from Congress to carry out this full investigation. Because up until now, this has all been so murky, and part of the reason why this has been a stop-and-go, even though those of us in the China AI space have been hearing about this for a while.

Companies like Megaspeed, their role in all this, even people like Alice Huang, have been flagged much earlier than this. The fact that this is coming out now, but also that the investigation was stopped and started within the Trump administration, is a big red flag. Ultimately, from Nvidia’s  standpoint, they’re going to have to come clean with whatever Congress now requests. There are going to be a lot of hard questions from Congress, as there should be, that have been building up for some time now.

If you ever looked at Jensen’s approach to chip export controls, he’s been very fiery that chip export controls are stupid. You mentioned earlier that’s in his business interest. It is better for the Chinese AI industry to be dependent on CUDA and dependent on Nvidia chips, because then if we do get into some conflict, maybe you can restrict that access and you’ll set them back. There’s some swirl of argument that he makes that says it’s in the United States’ national security interest to ship as many Nvidia GPUs to China as you can.

Then there are a lot of China hawks who are saying, “Actually, you need to restrain them and keep them years behind. They will not catch up to our bleeding-edge technology. Jensen, you just keep us ahead.” It feels like, out of all of this, the China hawks are going to start winning more fights than they’re losing — arguing that the Chinese government is actively trying to impede our efforts or actively trying to influence our government.

How should people think about that? What framework should we use to evaluate that mass of differing opinions, especially now that there’s a catalyst for some kind of change?

I think that’s the right way to frame up this whole debate. You have, on the one hand, folks who see the US-China AI competition as a critical strategic competition and access to compute is one of the key levers there, and thus US export controls, not only as they stand now, but tightening them further will be critical to maintaining US edge in the most powerful technology of our lives.

Then there are other people who are in the opposite camp who advocate for greater exports of the US AI tech stack writ large, including Nvidia chips and including to China. Up until now, that camp has been led by people like [Commerce Secretary] Howard Lutnick, Jensen Huang, and Trump himself. What’s interesting is the balance of power, in terms of whose arguing gets more weight, has been shifting and will shift in light of this recent controversy.

So here now those who have been advocating for more exports and fewer export controls, some of their arguments have been tainted by this process potentially, regardless of where the investigation goes.

Then there’s a final variable in all this, which is China itself. That’s something that matters a lot in this discussion because in the background, China is doing two things. One, they’re trying to build their own chips and they’re sort of all-in on building a resilient semiconductor supply chain with their own, say, Huawei AI chips that their own AI companies can use. They will never really catch up. It looks highly unlikely, but they could develop good enough chips to replace the Nvidia ones that they have been dependent on for so long.

The second big factor from China is retaliation. And this is one thing that I’m watching very closely. If these greater export controls are placed by the US on not just chips to China, but also on chip-making equipment — the tools required to make the semiconductors themselves — will China use its own export controls, such as restricting rare earth metals, to hit back?

Right. This is in the context of an ongoing trade and tariff war that has rocked the United States’ economy. In many ways, the first thing that Democrats should do when they enter the next Congress is pass a law getting rid of all the Trump tariffs, right? They’re brought into Congress to fix affordability and the tariffs are an affordability problem, and now we’re going to rush into a trade war with China because we might ask the Dutch government to restrict ASML chip making machines.

That seems very fraught to say, “We need to enter into an even more heated AI war with China that might result in the Chinese government placing export controls on the goods that you already find unaffordable.” Do you think that there’s the political will to go through this whole exercise, or is it just to punish Nvidia and Jensen Huang?

In some ways, this is happening against the backdrop of other issues that are probably more top of mind for both voters and for incoming legislators in the Capitol. Things like cost of living, as you point out, tariffs, and trying to investigate the Trump administration more broadly for corruption and other issues. Somewhere in there is also the debate around data centers and AI itself.

So in some ways, I’ll be curious to see how far this goes, the particular Nvidia issue. There is a scenario where a congressional investigation comes and goes, potentially finds no wrongdoing on Jensen Huang’s part, and then this is just folded into the longer debate around export controls. But there’s another world where if there are issues that come up, that could be potentially disruptive, not just for Nvidia and not just for the US-China relationship, but also for the AI boom in the US overall.

Tell me more about China itself. You mentioned that their chips will maybe get good enough. There’s an argument that the models right now, the frontier models we have today, are actually good enough to disrupt the economy. They’re certainly good enough to disrupt the field of mathematics.

You could stop training new models and just let the technology diffuse and you would still disrupt huge swaths of the economy today. We’re nowhere close to that actually happening. I think the AI labs should prove that they can do it with the technology they have today. That’s for another time.

But China doesn’t need to compete at the frontier to gain the productivity advantages and to gain the industrial advantages. The example I keep using is 5G. I was told for a decade that we had to win the race to 5G, otherwise China would do something and no one would ever tell me what the “something” was.

What is the “something” with AI that China will defeat us at that has made this such a critical geopolitical chess match? And is there a point where it will just be good enough for them to achieve that “something”?

The funny thing is that China doesn’t see this AI race as being so much about the frontier per se. They’re really much more focused on diffusing the technology. And they think they can “win” the AI race by just having AI used much more broadly and integrated throughout the economy, especially in areas like manufacturing where they are already the behemoth.

I think when they see the discussion around getting to AGI, certainly from the government standpoint in Beijing, that to them looks like a bubble and a waste of money. Why are you building all that compute for that? What’s interesting to see is the strategy as they’ve been playing it out is one where they’re trying to not fall too far behind the US, but really focus a lot more on trying to get — especially these open source models — out there across the Chinese economy and globally as well. To that extent, on that metric, they seem to be doing well.

That, to me, always has seemed like the real fight. Anthropic and OpenAI are furious that the Chinese companies are constantly distilling their models. They’re trying to build some technology to keep them from distilling their models.

But if you believe in the promise of AI and what it can do to the economy, your emphasis should be on diffusing good enough models, not AGI. Whereas our emphasis due to the way our market works is a bunch of guys who think they’re going to build digital Jesus. Whatever is going to happen, that’s the thing they want. [Anthropic CEO] Dario Amodei has to pretend that he cares about Salesforce, but we know what his real priority is.

How do the United States and China compete in that dynamic, where you have one very managed economy that has set a much more near-term and potentially achievable goal, and then our market system where the incentives of the leading market players have nothing to do with the economic incentives of the rest of us?

There’s even an ideological foundation to all of this because the vision of AGI is one that is so deeply embedded right now in the American AI community and Silicon Valley culture that I think there’s a risk of potential disconnect, not just between the US and China on this issue, but also within the US, between those who are in the labs like Anthropic and those who are outside who are saying, “Why are we building these giant metal boxes in our backyards? We don’t really see the point of this.”

So there’s already that divergence there. Part of it is this longstanding obsession in the American AI imagination with getting to the machine god essentially.

Bringing that all back to the context of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, Alice Huang, and Megaspeed. Megaspeed is a data center provider in Southeast Asia. It’s theoretically their business. They’re building data centers, they’re buying these chips. Shouldn’t market forces just end this?

The United States AI companies want to build data centers. They will pay whatever rates because they have an ideological purpose that is disconnected from capitalism potentially. The Chinese government is just trying to diffuse AI into manufacturing and the United States government would like to hold them back.

Shouldn’t market forces just mean that you sell the chips to the highest bidder and the highest bidder will almost always be an American AI company?

That’s an interesting question, because there is ultimately market demand in China still for these Nvidia chips. And there’s a divergence here between the companies in China who still want access to Nvidia chips and the government who is saying, “No, no, no. Why don’t you try Chinese chips? Why don’t you help us with our Chinese domestic chip development?”

There’s that divergence there. What’s interesting is players like Megaspeed in between could potentially do things like not just allow Chinese AI companies, again, to potentially get access to Nvidia chips, but then the argument some people are making is that those are chips that could have gone to the US AI companies and hyperscalers who are desperate.

That is an argument that’s out there, but fundamentally, I don’t know how much of this is driven by those sheer commercial interests alone or, again, by some of these policy or ideological divides.

Or by the influence of an alleged spy.

Right, exactly.

Because in a pure market environment, I think I know how this goes, but then you obviously have the complicated geopolitical dynamics and then you have this corruption element where both governments are attempting to influence one company at the center of the storm.

What do you think happens if the Nvidia board investigation determines that Jensen acted inappropriately or a shareholder lawsuit imposes massive liability on Nvidia or a congressional investigation?

There’s no way this company comes out of this unscathed, and the options are Jensen steps down or Nvidia’s restrained in some way or export controls go up even higher. Walk us through the probabilities and what you think happens next.

There is a scenario actually where this ends up with not that much happening.

Interesting.

There is a pathway where there is a congressional investigation and they possibly find no wrongdoing or maybe Jensen really didn’t know, as he claims, that this Alice Huang person was a Chinese spy, and that this ends up feeding into the longer standing trajectory of all the export control debates and everything like that. That’s one possibility.

Another possibility, though, is if there is some kind of wrongdoing that’s found, Jensen Huang might have to step down as CEO. He’s not just like a central node, he is like American AI, like the pillar that is holy.

He’s the only one making the dollar. I mean, this is very important.

Yeah, it’s like if you could draw the network diagram of the entire US AI ecosystem, Nvidia would be at the center of that. If you could draw the diagram of the entire Nvidia ecosystem, a single man is standing at the heart of all of that.

The question becomes, if he were no longer the CEO of Nvidia, how much impact would that have on Nvidia’s ability to make progress on its own AI chips and what impact would that have on the rest of the US AI industry? One possibility, for example, is that there is a slowdown in Nvidia’s ability to crank out next generation after next generation of better and better chips. And that could impact US overall compute build out. That is one possibility.

Another possibility is that there’s just so much demand and that the knowledge is diffused enough throughout Nvidia that the company can still continue to make progress at a breakneck pace even without their fearless leader at the top. A lot is unknown.

“Fearless” is the right word, because when I look at Nvidia, again, I don’t think Jensen is designing the chips. I know that there’s a character he wants to play, where he’s in all the meetings and he’s probably taking some risk in chip design that is hard for us to see from the outside.

But what we can see is Jensen’s enormous appetite for risk when it comes to financing neoclouds and investing in frontier AI companies. All of the dollars Nvidia is making flow back out in a circle to the AI ecosystem. It’s unclear to me whether that continues to happen without Jensen specifically being willing to front the risk and show up on CNBC as the face of the risk and say, “Everything’s okay.” What do you think happens then?

His role as not just a technology leader, but as a market maker is really crucial. When he calls out certain companies like certain startups or neoclouds, you can see their stock prices go up. When he says something like, “I don’t know if this quantum thing is going to work out,” you saw the entire industry takes a hit. So that is the weight of his role in the broader ecosystem.

Going forward, without that kind of advocate and this market maker playing this active role, that’s another factor. Beyond the Nvidia chips themselves and the technological role of the company, there is this deeper industry or even sociological function that Jensen plays and that Nvidia plays in this broader AI buildout.

One of the interesting dynamics in all of that is Jensen also doesn’t seem to care very much about AGI. He thinks it’s just software. I’ve heard him say, “This is just software. Everybody calm down. These risks are fake. We don’t need a safety regime, all this stuff.” He’s more aligned with what you’re describing as the Chinese viewpoint, where this is just a tool to accelerate our economy. If he goes, maybe that changes too.

It’s possible. He has been one of the most powerful counterweights to the “let’s go all in on AGI” perspective that you hear from Dario Amodei and Sam Altman, for example. Without his voice in that process, he’s also been a very strong advocate for open source. Again, emphasizing the diffusion rather than the, say, control and restrictions on cutting-edge AI.

I do think if his voice is not there, there would be a pretty big vacuum for folks who would advocate that position or that view. At the same time though, again, beyond the immediate AI industry in the US, I don’t know how much that “race to AGI” argument resonates with the broader US public.

Right now a lot of people are just more wondering about the nuts and bolts of it. Is this technology going to cost me my job tomorrow? Is it actually useful? Is it impacting my university studies? Those are things that maybe are more impactful day-to-day for most ordinary Americans.

It is abundantly clear that Jensen is not a great spokesperson to the average consumer in the United States. He has not made the sale to them. He’s made the sale to a bunch of financiers. He’s made the sale to Wall Street. He’s made the sale to the tech industry.

But the average American, as we can just see from the polling in the election, is very, very skeptical of all of this and very, very skeptical of the costs versus the benefits. Again, I’m just putting that in the context of there’s an alleged Chinese spy whispering in the ear of this man.

What truly would the Chinese government hope to gain from that? Because in one way, they’ve actually achieved a victory here. They’ve destabilized the American AI economy. But it doesn’t seem like that was the goal. They’re furiously denying that any of this even happened.

There is another very counterintuitive take, which is they kind of shot themselves in the foot on this one. From Beijing’s perspective, they don’t want to see more export controls, they might want to see a loosening. But now because of this potential Chinese spy, they’ve tainted the one man who has been advocating the most for loosening export controls. In some ways now, they’ve taken out someone who had otherwise for sheer commercial reasons been more aligned, and who’s going to take that place?

If anything now, it has really charged the Democrats especially, who have been criticizing the Trump administration about not being tougher on these export controls. It has really galvanized the Democrats on this front and made it more of an issue perhaps than it was before.

Yeah, especially when you connect it to corruption and the AI industry wasting money, all this stuff, it’s all there for them. Tell me more broadly about Chinese spying in the AI industry.

There was a report, I don’t know, a few months ago that OpenAI was warning its employees that spies abound, that if suddenly attractive people appeared, be wary because they were probably spies. I love that. There’s just something about that that’s great.

Obviously when it hits Jensen, it’s a different kind of story, especially with the national security implications and corruption implications. Give us a sense of what the spy trade is like on the ground for the average AI researcher.

All I can say here is that they are juicy targets. For the US AI labs, anyone who’s involved with cutting-edge frontier AI,  chip production, and chip design would be juicy targets for Chinese intelligence gathering because this is something where China’s trying to catch up. They’re trying to figure out how to keep pace with the US on AI and try to build their own alternatives to Nvidia GPUs.

You can see there have been other examples of cases where they’ve been poaching engineers from TSMC in Taiwan or from South Korea, and have struggled to deal with efforts to hold back this strategic IP basically. There’s probably a lot more happening under the surface in terms of this cat-and-mouse game, but I do think that they are prime targets.

Correct me if I’m wrong, but I think that there have been warnings from the US government to be careful and to step up your game on the cybersecurity front and the intelligence front to protect against these threats.

Meanwhile, they’re putting all their information into Slack and getting breached on the daily. Who knows if these warnings are taking off.

Onto the last set of questions here — I’m thinking about Apple and Tesla, where we moved our manufacturing to China and we moved our supply chains to China, the Chinese industries.

Whether it was above board or not — and there’s a rich debate you could have on that, we’ve had it on the show — they learned a lot from our companies. There was technology transfer. That’s happening in AI too.

There are a lot of Chinese AI researchers working in and around these labs. There is technology transfer happening, again, above board or not. Isn’t that just the normal course of business or is there something more nefarious happening here?

To some extent there are people flows and knowledge flows. You might not even think of it in terms of national-level AI communities. You might think about this global diffusion of know-how tips and tricks for squeezing a bit more performance out of the same amount of compute. Especially up until recently, you saw a lot of sharing of, say, papers like the transformer paper, that disseminated new architectural breakthroughs throughout the global AI community. And now that’s changing, obviously, as a lot of companies, especially the US companies, are holding this much closer to their chest.

But there is this broader question about who gets access to this. Who gains and loses? I guess it’s also not just a one-way flow. Some of these American AI companies benefit a lot from having some of these Chinese developers work with them. In the same way Apple and Tesla, it wasn’t just like they gave away the crown jewels to China, but that China in turn saved these companies, especially at times when they were facing a perilous moment in their histories.

There’s this bigger question about what the line is between normal commercial and technology flows versus a concerted state-backed effort to obtain sensitive strategic secrets and IP technology that would have broader geopolitical implications.

Does that strategy for China look like a bunch of companies like Megaspeed with allegedly compromised executives, or does it play out more directly?

Actually if anything, it would be less about the companies like Megaspeed, who seem to be middlemen for dealing with compute, and perhaps different companies, different agencies perhaps in the Chinese system, that might be more active.

At one extreme you have the outright concerted efforts at industrial espionage. They’re state-backed actors who are very systematic at trying to obtain some of the best commercial secrets from around the world, including from American companies.

But on the other hand, you do also have this gray zone of, “If a Chinese company acquires a stake in a US or European company, what does that mean? Does that mean they’re trying to obtain the technology or is that a regular commercial deal?” That’s where it starts to get more difficult to parse and you’d have to look at it on a case-by-case basis.

One of the dynamics in talking about the Chinese government and the United States, especially when you talk to American industrialists, is that the American government is chaos and democracy is messy and everyone’s running in 50 different directions, and the Chinese system is directed. They make 100-year plans, not one-quarter plans. We’ve heard it. Everyone knows these cliches.

How true is that? In this case alone, it doesn’t seem like they achieved the goal of their plan. In many cases, they might have actually set themselves back.

Oh, yeah. For those who actually study China, who have done long-term research on this country and who understand it more closely, it looks like a much messier picture than any of these portrayals, especially from those in Silicon Valley who try to juxtapose China against what they find to be this annoyingly messy and unruly democracy.

The Chinese system, both within the government and then across industries and government, is full of conflicting interests, rife with corruption. There are lots of times where you have bureaucratic turf wars that spill out into the open. You have missteps, ones that can backfire profoundly.

You see that all the time. You see the local governments not following what Beijing wants, or following what Beijing wants but in the wrong direction. Sometimes they’re given a signal and they say, “Oh, okay, we got to run that way.” And then Beijing says, “No, no, no, no, no, other way, other way.”

This happens all the time, and to anyone in Silicon Valley who’s trying to make this “neat” argument, all I can say is, go talk to people in China. They can tell you how messy it actually is on the ground.

Kyle, this has been great. What do you think will happen next year? What should people be looking out for?

The biggest thing is a congressional investigation and who’s behind that, what that surface is. And then potentially along with that, these pending bills around export controls and whether those will now get more momentum to pass in Congress, and whether Trump himself, and the White House in general, will try to play a role in either stopping that or giving that a quiet green light.

I suspect we’re going to want to talk to you again as this process plays out. Thank you so much, Kyle, for being on Decoder.

Thank you.

articles.title: CRPF Post Attack Triggers Fresh Search Operation in Jammu and Kashmir
articles.text:
Security forces on Thursday resumed the search operation in Jammu and Kashmir’s Kulgam district to track down two terrorists, who attacked a CRPF post injuring three personnel, officials said.
Two heavily armed terrorists emerged from a dense cluster of trees and opened fire at a Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) post in the South Kashmir district on Wednesday, injuring three CRPF personnel, one of them critically.
The two men disappeared into the forested area after the attack that took place around 2.15 pm near Mir Bazar, about 75 km from Srinagar and just a km from the strategic Jammu-Srinagar National Highway.
Immediately after the attack, security launched a massive cordon and search operation in the area to track down the terrorists. On Thursday morning, the security forces resumed the searches, the officials said.They said the forces have erected barricades and deployed armoured vehicles at several places in the district.
Checking and frisking of vehicles is being undertaken at the security check-points as a tight vigil is being maintained.

articles.title: Russian University Plans Drone Factory Technology Transfer to India
articles.text:
Russia is set to send technology for making unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to India as part of a deal between Tomsk State University (TSU) and a Russian drone production centre in the Tomsk region.
TSU Rector Eduard Galazhinsky told the ‘Industry Code’ conference in Tomsk on November 11, via Russia’s TASS news agency, that the Russian university and Tomsk region’s Scientific and Production Centre for Unmanned Aircraft Systems were set to sign a deal with an Indian partner.
The Indian side will pay for the technology and factory, whilst the Russian entities will provide a full suite of technological solutions. Russia will also receive royalties from sales made.
Galazhinsky noted that instead of an export deal, the deal would involve technology transfer, giving the Indian partner their own production line whilst providing an ongoing financial benefit for the Russian university and production centre.
The exact Indian organisation or entity involved in negotiations have not been specified. Nor have the UAVs’ type, specification, military or civil use, nor how much will be invested into the facility.
The Russian side however do have a robust industry and research base. The Scientific and Production Centre for Unmanned Aircraft Systems in Tomsk region was opened in February 2025 with help from federal and regional funding. The centre can design, prototype, produce and flight test UAVs.
They have designed a 50Kw engine for drones made domestically and produced a limited run of high payload UAVs weighing up to 200kg. They also have additive manufacturing capabilities and flight testing.
This could provide the Indian partner with access to a greater variety of production technologies. Although it is not clear if the 200kg UAV or 50Kw engine will be part of the technology transfer.
For India this could be another step in expanding their UAV production base by partnering with foreign technology. Instead of importing fully built aircraft, they can develop their own skills in assembling, producing parts, testing and maintaining. This will depend on what technology is being transferred, what intellectual property is involved and how many parts are produced domestically.
The royalty arrangement also shows that the Russians will have an ongoing interest in the production in India. This could mean that there is an ongoing relationship where products will be sold, upgraded and supported.
Whilst this is part of a wider effort to increase cooperation between India and Russia over UAVs, technology transfer, localisation and training, this should not be mistaken for a state defence deal or confirmed procurement by the Indian military.
The deal needs to be signed and we need to know who the Indian partner is, what UAV they have chosen and what technology will be transferred. Until then this is just a potential industry partnership.

articles.title: United Airlines wants you to check in, not your chatbot
articles.text:
United Airlines has become the latest company to slap restrictions on unauthorized third-party AI agents, warning that the bots could make unintended purchases, expose customer data, or bypass checks requiring human acknowledgment.

The airline announced restrictions covering both its own digital platforms and indirect access through travel agencies and aggregators, with changes to its booking, ticketing, and distribution policies.

United says automated actions could violate aviation regulations, citing the requirement for a human acknowledgment during check-in that bags contain no banned substances. A bot cheerfully ticking the box isn't quite the passenger confirmation it has in mind.

And then there is the worry that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."

United would also rather customers use its own app than turn third-party assistants loose on its systems.

AI agents are pitched as a way to outsource life's minutiae, and it's difficult to navigate the web without tripping over a breathless influencer explaining why you need one, or dozens, or hundreds of virtual personal assistants.

The thing is that operating these assistants requires care and thought. Earlier this year, British mathematician Professor Hannah Fry conducted a cautionary experiment in which she gave an AI agent a bank card, and a bit too much agency, to see what it would do. Passwords were coughed up, and some ill-considered purchases were made. Still, as Fry said of the agent, dubbed Cassandra, "don't let her incompetence fool you, because these things are getting better fast."

Last month, reports emerged of major US banks blocking third-party AI agents from operating inside accounts and taking actions on behalf of the customer. This month, several UK banks were reported to have followed suit.

United stated: "Corporate leaders in the banking and retail industries have taken similar actions regarding AI agents and we encourage others to consider measures that preserve the data and security of their customers and strengthen safety."

The Register asked United Airlines how it planned to implement the blocking. There are a few options, including physical biometric confirmation for actions or checking for signs of automated browser driving. Amazon has also moved against unauthorized AI agents, blocking Meta's Muse (the "AI that gets it done," according to Meta's marketing) in September.

The airline has yet to respond. ®

Kaveri’s Russian Trials Expose India’s Testing Gap Says Chinese Analysts
articles.text:
India’s recent success in achieving 48.5kN of dry thrust in the Russian trials of the Kaveri Derivative Engine (KDE) has caused some scepticism in Chinese Defence Circles. While India has seemingly overcome their issues with aero-engines, the question being asked is whether New Delhi even has the infrastructure in place to perform independent testing and certification.
Recent reports revealed that the DRDO’s Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE) had completed high altitude and flight testing of the non-afterburning Kaveri Derivative Engine at Russia’s CIAM and Gromov Flight Research Institute. The engine produced 48.5kN of maximum dry thrust, beating its target of around 46kN.
While this is important news for the Ghatak UCAV programme (as the dry engine is being developed), it doesn’t mean that the engine has passed the certification stage. The test data will need to be analysed by CEMILAC before the engine can be certified and integrated onto the platform.
China’s iFeng website asked why there was so much celebration surrounding the event. They noted that it was a non-afterburning derivative and that India had “not solved the real problem” but had progressed on a simpler version of the engine. It highlighted that India has developed a working prototype but not a high performance engine.
Wforum had a more detailed look at the issue. They pointed out that India do not have any independent testing facilities as the latest round of tests were all performed in Russia.
This could cause issues if changes need to be made to the prototype. Engineers would need to send the engine back to Russia to get it tested again. This can cause delays and increase costs.
A lack of a fully indigenous high altitude testing facility has been well known to be an issue with India’s aerospace development. It has previously been recognised in parlimentary documents that India lacked testing facilities meaning that the original Kaveri engine suffered from delays. The government noted that “Critical altitude testing and flying test bed testing has been carried out abroad”.
But it is not true to say that the Kaveri engine hasn’t been flight tested. The original Kaveri engine had completed 27 flights and 57 hours of testing on an IL-76 flying test bed at the Gromov Flight Research Institute. As well as ground testing, the engine has been developed in India.
The Chinese commentary also raised concerns over whether India do have the independent capability to verify all of the data from the Russian tests. While this isn’t necessarily true, the certification process should ensure that the engine meets the required standards for airworthiness.
There are also issues with the money spent on the Kaveri engine. While China have mentioned some figures, some figures need correcting. The original project was sanctioned in 1989 with a cost of ₹382.81 crore and was later increased to ₹2,839 crore. In 2021, a parliamentary answer stated that the total amount spent was ₹2,035.56 crore, compared to the ₹2,105 crore that was allocated.
The Chinese often compare the Kaveri engine with China’s WS-10 engine. They argue that China took a flawed early version of their engine, put it into service and continued to improve it whereas the Kaveri engine never went into production for the Tejas. While this is a valid point, it shouldn’t be said that the Kaveri engine has never been flight tested. The original engine has been tested on a flying test bed. It just never had the service experience of a production fighter engine.
Issues with the Chinese commentary include many of the articles from Wforum, Toutiao and Kunlunce seem to be based on the same Indian commentary. Many of the reports regarding the September tests in Russia seem to be based on Indian Defence Media.
The most important takeaway from this is that India need to develop a full ecosystem for developing indigenous engines. This includes high altitude testing facilities, component testing, flying test beds, materials knowledge and independent certification.

articles.title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia chief executive
articles.text:
Nvidia's Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of the company, following the revelation of his affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy and reports of a relationship with another woman who was a company employee.

In a Form 8-K [PDF] filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the GPU maker disclosed that it accepted the resignation of Huang, whom it identified as Jen-Hsun Huang, on November 11, effective immediately.

He is being replaced by chief financial officer Colette Kress, who will serve as interim leader while the board conducts a search for a new CEO.

Huang, who founded Nvidia in 1993 and served as president, CEO, and a member of the board of directors ever since, led the GPU maker to become one of the most valuable companies in the world, hitting a hit peak of over $5.5 trillion earlier this year.

His position became untenable following an investigation by the company's board after he admitted to an affair, amid allegations he had a romantic relationship with a woman the US authorities suspected as a Chinese spy.

Reports later surfaced this week of a second alleged affair with an employee of the company itself, reported by the New York Times as being with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care.

A two-week downfall

News of the scandal first broke barely a couple of weeks ago, on October 29, when claims surfaced that Huang had been the target of an espionage plot involving a Chinese businesswoman working for a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed which was a customer of Nvidia.

According to the New York Times, US intelligence had reason to believe the woman, Alice Huang, was recruited to gather information about Nvidia and its operations for the Beijing government. Megaspeed also faces claims it was illicitly shipping Nvidia products to China, in violation of US export controls.

Any relationship between Huang and a Chinese operative would be enormously concerning, as the US has been trying to keep advanced technology for AI out of the hands of the country, allegedly for security reasons, fearing it might be used for military purposes.

For its part, Beijing rejects the spying allegations, saying they are part of a smear campaign against China.

Shortly after Nvidia’s board announced it was investigating Huang, he sent an email to Nvidia staff apologizing and confessing to having an affair, though he did not explicitly name Alice Huang in his public apology.

It seemed like the leather-jacketed leader might just hang on, since it was difficult to imagine anyone other than him leading the company after all this time. But Nvidia’s shares fell 4.3 percent on November 9 and a further 5.5 percent the following day, wiping around $430 billion off its market value, amid all the speculation.

Then the claim emerged regarding a second affair, with an employee at Nvidia who reported to him, and many commentators took it as a sign the game was up. Huang resigned the same day the news broke.

Indecision ahead

Now the speculation starts over who will take over the reins at Nvidia, but Huang could prove a tough act to follow. He is said to have recognized early on the potential for taking the number-crunching capabilities of graphics processors and putting them to use at accelerating AI processing, and Nvidia’s position today as the leading AI hardware firm is thanks to that bet.

“The sudden resignation of Jensen Huang is about more than succession at the world’s most important AI chipmaker, Nvidia’s leadership crisis is a stress test for the AI boom,” says Forrester VP and group research director Stephanie Balaouras.

If Nvidia stabilizes quickly under new leadership, the AI infrastructure boom will have demonstrated resilience, she adds. But if its stock or financing relationships remain under sustained pressure, that would add evidence to the fragility of the AI bubble.

“In the near term, the board did the sensible thing and reached for a steward. Colette Kress knows every number in that order book,” commented Mark Malek, CIO at financial services firm Siebert Financial.

“It does NOT settle the stock. Interim means the real decision is still ahead, the investigations are still open, and next week’s earnings call just became the most important in the company’s history,” he added. ®

Quantum leap: IBM plans to scale beyond 1,000 qubits in 2027 with Nighthawk r3 processor
articles.text:
IBM has unveiled the Nighthawk r3, an upcoming next-gen quantum processor that will feature 520 qubits, as another step towards a planned fault-tolerant quantum system it hopes to launch in 2029.

Big Blue's current Nighthawk r2 was only made available in September and features 120 quantum bits (qubits) capable of handling circuits using 7,500 operations.

Its successor, IBM claims, will have more than four times as many qubits and execute 10,000 quantum operations to tackle larger, more complex problems while maintaining the same speed and accuracy.

Nighthawk r3 is slated to arrive in 2027, when Big Blue plans to link two of the quantum processors into a single system with more than 1,000 qubits.

IBM said applications increasingly require circuits executing thousands of quantum operations on approximately 100 qubits or more, speeding up collection of the millions or billions of samples needed to perform complex computations. Speed determines whether such demanding workloads can be completed in practical timeframes and at a reasonable cost.

The new quantum processor will feature 10 chip-to-chip interconnects, called l-couplers, designed for linking together processors that it will use to enable a single 1,040-qubit system. This tech was tested using Nighthawk r1 processors.

IBM previously outlined its goal of reaching reliable error correcting territory in 2029 with a quantum processor codenamed Starling. Now it intends for this to be the world’s first fault-tolerant quantum computer, capable of running quantum circuits comprising 100 million quantum operations on 200 logical qubits.

This is an ambitious goal, considering fault-tolerant quantum technology always seems to be at least a decade away, despite numerous breakthroughs and technology introductions. However, some in the technology industry believe the odds on a working system are shortening, given the increased activity around making encryption ready with support for quantum-resistant algorithms.

Then again, a professor at the University of Auckland New Zealand famously claimed last year that quantum computers hadn't so far managed to factor any number greater than 21 without cheating.

IBM presented a framework for Starling in a 2025 paper outlining hardware to implement the improbably named bivariate bicycle quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) error correction codes. These significantly reduce the number of physical qubits needed to store and process quantum information, compared to existing surface codes.

Using the architecture in the paper, Big Blue intends to assemble Starling from modules that each contain a quantum memory and logical processing unit (LPU), allowing logic operations on the memory. The modules will have universal adapters letting them connect using l-couplers.

IBM is also preparing the way ahead by combining its quantum processors with classical high-performance compute (HPC) systems to research better quantum error correction.

Last week, Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) in the US announced such a system, combining an IBM Quantum System Two with Nighthawk r2 quantum processors and Umbra, powered by AMD 5th Gen Epyc CPUs and Instinct MI355X GPU accelerators.

IBM also has a partnership with Japan's RIKEN scientific research institute under which an IBM Quantum System Two has been integrated with the Fugaku Arm-based supercomputer, once the most powerful system in the world. ®

articles.title: Why the L&T-BEL Consortium Looks Strong in the AMCA Race
articles.text:
L&T-Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL)-Dynamatic Technologies consortium is one of the most-watched entries in the race to design the prototype of India’s Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA). The consortium offers a wide range of strengths. Larsen & Toubro (L&T) has the complex engineering, systems integration and project managment skills, whilst Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) has strong competencies in military electronics, radar, electronic warfare and communication systems. Dynamatic Technologies brings complex manufacturing capabilities.
Dynamatic joined the L&T-BEL partnership in November 2025 as an exclusive partner for the AMCA programme. The partnership combines L&T’s engineering abilities, BEL’s electronics capabilities and Dynamatic’s complex aerostructures and subsystems manufacturing capabilities.
This ensures they have a wide range of manufacturing capabilities. In order to manufacture five flying prototypes and a structural test aircraft, close coordination between structural manufacturing, avionics, electronics, testing and aircraft integration are required.
A key aspect of their partnership is that during BEL’s Q2 FY2026-27 earnings call, Chairman and Managing Director Manoj Jain confirmed that BEL had partnered with L&T and that the bid had been made with L&T leading as an exclusive partnership, with 50% split between both companies. Dynamatic has joined the partnership as an exclusive partner.
“This is a very competitive bid. We are hopeful that we will come out as the lowest bidder (L1). The technical evaluation can take anywhere between 2-3 months. It is possible that the price bid may be opened before March 2027. But this is just an estimate and it is entirely up to the ADA to decide,” Jain added.
Whilst it shows BEL are confident with their bid, this does not mean they have passed technical evaluation, nor that they will win as L1.
The AMCA prototype will be a challenging task for the rival consortia. As the programme will be government funded and costs an estimated ₹15,000 crore to build, the winning consortium will be required to form a new company within 3 months of winning. This new company will have to manufacture a greenfield site at Puttaparthi, Andhra Pradesh.
The RFP requires the first prototype to fly within 30 months of signing the contract. The programme will involve manufacturing 5 flying prototypes, 1 structural test aircraft and 1,800 flight test sorties within 84 months. This would place great demands on project management, manufacturing, supply chain and working capital.
L&T’s large scale and experience with complex engineering projects could prove to be an advantage. BEL will bring a major public sector defence electronics partner, and Dynamatic brings a well-established aerospace manufacturing base. However, all 3 companies will need to work together as a team with L&T leading the project.
The consortium will face competition from Tata Advanced Systems and Bharat Forge-BEML-Data Patterns. Both will bring their own manufacturing strengths but ultimately it will come down to technical and commercial evaluation.

articles.title: Hackers exploiting ScreenConnect plugin flaw to spread malware across hundreds of PCs
articles.text:
Hackers have used a dodgy third-party ScreenConnect extension to push malware onto at least 288 machines across 48 organizations, prompting ConnectWise to disable a handful of plugins in hundreds of customer environments.

Security outfit Huntress first raised the alarm in a Reddit post on Wednesday, warning of an active campaign targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances. At the time, its security operations center was tracking six compromised managed service providers (MSPs) and more than 286 affected endpoints, with the numbers still climbing.

ConnectWise acquired popular remote supporttool ScreenConnect in February, 2015.

Huntress spotted the attacks at around 1747 UTC, when someone began using ScreenConnect's remote command feature to install rogue clients on machines managed by multiple IT service providers. All 288 endpoints were hit within 90 minutes, with roughly a third compromised in the first ten minutes.

Huntress suspects more MSPs may have been compromised, as the attackers appeared to be numbering their victims sequentially, with the numbers suggesting earlier attacks that it hadn't detected.

The attackers deployed a 16-file malware toolkit dubbed SCKit, which installs a separate ScreenConnect client to maintain remote access even if the legitimate connection is shut down. It also contains code designed to spread the infection to IT technicians and potentially other customers under their control.

Huntress has since traced the activity to a possible authentication weakness in RMM+, a third-party extension that lets other management tools issue commands through ScreenConnect without technicians using its console.

Versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of the extension contain a flaw that means installations without a configured access key will accept a blank one. Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands without defeating MFA.

Huntress said the findings matched what its investigators saw during the attacks, with commands reaching machines across several ScreenConnect installations despite no corresponding login activity.

The researchers also confirmed that the attacks affected ScreenConnect versions 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783, meaning administrators running the latest releases weren't necessarily safe.

ConnectWise has acknowledged that third-party extensions may have been involved but has stopped short of confirming how the attackers initially gained access.

In a security advisory, the company said it was investigating unauthorized access to certain partner environments and had identified approximately 400 installations containing at least one extension from the RMM+ family.

It has disabled five extensions, including RMM+, RMM Plus, and Labtech Plus, wherever it can do so remotely, and urged customers running their own ScreenConnect servers to follow suit.

ConnectWise stressed that the 400 environments were identified because they had the extensions installed, not because they were necessarily compromised.

The company said: "At this time, we have found no evidence of a compromise of ConnectWise infrastructure or a vulnerability in ScreenConnect itself."

There's another nasty trick buried in SCKit. According to Huntress, the malware is designed to turn an infected computer into a trap for the technician sent to investigate it. If the technician connects through ScreenConnect, the toolkit attempts to transfer malware back to their workstation, steal authentication cookies, and use their access to infect other machines.

That could give attackers a route from one compromised customer into others managed by the same IT provider. However, Huntress says it has yet to see that part of the attack succeed.

"We have not observed that method to spread work successfully. The console-takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log we have checked so far," the researchers wrote.

Huntress also suspects that some of the malware's C# code was generated using an LLM, pointing to unusually detailed comments explaining what the code is supposed to do. Apparently, even malware authors appreciate a little help with their homework.

Both Huntress and ConnectWise are urging administrators not to investigate suspected infections by remotely connecting through ScreenConnect, since doing so could put the technician's own machine at risk.

Administrators are being advised to use other security tools to investigate affected machines, look for rogue ScreenConnect clients, and check what commands have been run. Any malware left behind will also need to be removed before the machines are brought back online.

Huntress warned on Reddit that some machines were becoming reinfected within minutes of being taken out of isolation because the malware had not been properly removed.

Simply disabling the vulnerable extensions won't necessarily undo the damage, either. As ConnectWise warns, "Disabling extensions and resetting credentials alone may not remove unauthorized software, persistence mechanisms, or access already established on endpoints."

And with the attackers already able to install their own remote access software, kicking them out could prove considerably harder than closing the door they came through. ®
